answer.answer:
Designing for manufacture and assembly with robots starts in the design phase and rests on four things: highly standardised components, a modular product architecture, early contractor involvement and a parametric algorithm to carry the geometry. Only the last of those is a tool; the other three are properties of the design and a state of the project organisation, which is the real finding here. Once in place, design for manufacture and assembly orients the project toward prefabrication and modularisation, and robotic assembly then needs a robotic arm and prefabricated, unified parts before it needs anything else; standardisation is the one requirement that serves both the design method and the robot. Watch workforce training, which is what human-robot interaction depends on across most of the coded record, and note that no deployed project or firm sits in the material in front of me for this question, so this guidance rests on the literature rather than on a built case.

**Where design for manufacture and assembly sits**

PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" is a Process enabler, drawn on by 15 of the 50 coded cases [1]. It applies in the Design phase, spans Design through Structural Construction, and plays a design-for-X role [2]. The graph lists exactly six dependency edges on it, three inbound and three outbound, so what follows is the complete dependency picture for PR9 and can be read as a total.

**The four upstream requirements, which are not equal**

- AT7 "Highly standardised" (Attribute) enables PR9: design standardisation and simplification is a DfMA enabler for offsite construction, peer-reviewed, and the edge is carried by 13 of the 50 cases [1]. AT7 itself is drawn on by 25 of the 50 cases [1], the largest of the four.
- CO11 "Early contractor involvement" (Condition) enables PR9: early collaboration is among the DfMA enablers, carried by 11 of the 50 cases [1]; CO11 is drawn on by 14 cases [1].
- AT2 "Modular" (Attribute) enables PR9: alignment of product modularity and process modularity enhances DfMA capability [3], carried by 7 of the 50 cases [1]; AT2 is drawn on by 12 cases [1].
- PR9 dependsOn RE1 "Parametric/computational/data-driven algorithm/machine code" (Resource), so RE1 is upstream in practice: the DfMA-oriented process combines DfMA with BIM parametric design to support manufacture and assembly [4], carried by 8 of the 50 cases [1]; RE1 is drawn on by 11 cases [1].

Standardisation and modularity also reinforce each other: AT2 enables AT7 because modular architecture reduces the variety of component sizes produced (carried by 11 cases) [1], and AT7 enables AT2 through decoupled standardised interfaces (also 11 cases) [1]. Against them, AT1 "Bespoke/customised design" constrains AT2, since integral architecture couples functions tightly to components (carried by 4 cases) [1]: bespoke geometry is the thing that will cost you the modular route.

**What design for manufacture and assembly then delivers**

PR9 enables PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", orienting the project toward offsite manufacture [5], carried by 15 of the 50 cases, the strongest of PR9's outbound edges [1], and PR9 enables PR5 "Modularisation" as a DfMA principle [6], carried by 8 cases [1]. From there the customisation route opens: PR5 enables PR11 "Mass-customisation" (8 cases) [1], AR6 "Configurators/kit-of-parts" enables PR11 by integrating customisation data into robotic manufacturing [7] (9 cases) [1], and AT7 enables AR6, on standards evidence, since modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components (11 cases) [1]. Modularisation also opens entry for specialised module makers, enabling AC13 "Supplier/manufacturer" (10 cases) [1].

Prefabrication is where the returns are booked: PR2 enables VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency" (19 cases) [1], VA3 "Improve quality/performance" through the controlled factory environment (18 cases) [1], VA10 "Reduce errors/constraints" (14 cases) [1] and VA13 "Improve site safety" by moving work offsite (12 cases) [1]. It also carries obligations: PR2 dependsOn RI14 "Rely on precise planning" (18 cases) [1] and dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", since a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability (10 cases) [1].

**Adding the robot**

PR4 "Robotic assembly" is drawn on by 13 of the 50 cases [1]. Its requirements: PR4 dependsOn RE2 "Robotic arm" (12 cases) [1], RE2 being drawn on by 22 cases [1]; PR4 hasPrecondition PR2, because automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials (4 cases) [1]; AT7 enables PR4, with Japanese automated erection systems relying on standardised prefabricated components (10 cases) [1]; and PR12 "Path-planning" enables PR4 as a precondition (2 cases) [1]. PR4 also dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture", since robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context (2 cases) [1]. Returns: PR4 amplifies VA2 (13 cases) [1] and amplifies VA6 "Reduce cost" (7 cases) [1], while PR4 enabling VA10 "Reduce errors/constraints" through quality control [8] is carried by just 1 of the 50 cases [1], so the error-reduction claim for robotic assembly is thin in the record even though the claim for prefabrication is not.

One further path is asserted and unused: CO12 "Mobile factory", a Condition, enables PR4 on the argument that all-weather cover allows welding and assembly to proceed in a normal manner even in rain, and that edge is carried by 0 of the 50 coded cases [1]; CO12 is drawn on by 1 case [1]. Cited in the literature, carried by none of the 50.

**People, safety and regulation**

CO6 "Human-robot interaction" is drawn on by 32 of the 50 cases [1] and dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training", since the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce; that edge is carried by 27 of the 50 cases [1], the heaviest carried edge in this whole set. CO6 also dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" on standards evidence, compliance with robot safety standards (2 cases) [1], and mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern" through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits (4 cases) [1]. Treat training as the first cost of the robot, not the last.

**Extent of the evidence**

The retrieval widened "robotics" beyond robotic assembly, but that changes little: RE10 "Gantry-type robotic system" is drawn on by 5 cases and carries no dependency edges [1], so it contributes no requirement or outcome path here, and no record for an unmanned mobile vehicle is in front of me. More importantly, the context holds no deployed process record and no named firm bearing on this question, so nothing above rests on a built project; the edges are peer-reviewed or standards-based, and the case counts tell you how far each is exhibited in the 50-case record. The co-occurrence list is a top-15 cut of 2897 edges and the 1-hop expansion is a sample, so neither establishes that anything is absent.
